japanese_yoshiie.name: Pierce three men with one arrow
japanese_yoshiie.notes: Legendary archer whose drawn bow could drive a single shaft through three stacked men or three suits of armour, the deed that won him the byname Hachimantarō.

sources.reference: Ryōjin Hishō (imayō song collection); Heike Monogatari, Yoshiie episodes

japanese_yoshiie.name: Read the omen of the scattering geese
japanese_yoshiie.notes: At the Later Three-Years War he is said to have detected an ambush in the marsh of Kuriyagawa by noticing a line of wild geese break formation, a feat of military divination attached to his cult as patron of warriors.

sources.reference: Ōshū Gosannen Ki (Tale of the Later Three-Years War)

japanese_yoshitsune.name: Leap across eight boats (hassō-tobi)
japanese_yoshitsune.notes: At Dan-no-ura, hard pressed, he sprang from vessel to vessel across eight boats to escape the Taira warrior Noritsune, the canonical hassō-tobi.

sources.reference: Gikeiki (Chronicle of Yoshitsune); Heike Monogatari, Dan-no-ura

japanese_yoshitsune.name: Tengu-taught swordsmanship and tactics
japanese_yoshitsune.notes: As the boy Ushiwakamaru at Kurama-dera he was trained in the sword, tactics and magic by the tengu king Sōjōbō in the valley of Sōjōgatani.

sources.reference: Gikeiki (Chronicle of Yoshitsune); Noh play Kurama Tengu

japanese_yoshitsune.name: The cliff-descent at Hiyodorigoe
japanese_yoshitsune.notes: Led a surprise cavalry charge straight down the precipitous Hiyodori ravine to break the Taira at Ichi-no-Tani, the most celebrated of his tactical coups.

sources.reference: Heike Monogatari, Battle of Ichi-no-Tani

japanese_yoshinaka.name: The fire-ox night attack at Kurikara
japanese_yoshinaka.notes: Routed the much larger Taira army at the Kurikara Pass by stampeding oxen with torches bound to their horns down the slope in a night assault.

sources.reference: Heike Monogatari, Battle of Kurikara

javanese_semar.name: The all-conquering wind (kentut)
javanese_semar.notes: When finally roused, the lowly clown deploys his flatulence as an irresistible weapon that overcomes even the mightiest gods and demons, a comic inversion of his hidden supremacy as Sang Hyang Ismaya.

sources.reference: Javanese wayang kulit lakon repertoire; Semar tradition

ket_es.name: Cast the faithless Hosedem from heaven
ket_es.notes: As supreme sky-god Es flung his wife Hosedem out of the sky for her adultery with the Moon, sending her to dominate the cold north as the soul-devouring death-being.

sources.reference: V. I. Anuchin, materials on Ket (Yenisei-Ostyak) religion; E. A. Alekseenko, Ket ethnography

ket_es.name: Sender of thunder and the celestial order
ket_es.notes: Remote benign high-god of the uppermost heaven (Ket eś 'sky'), accessible chiefly to shamans, who maintains the order of the world and the heavens.

sources.reference: E. J. Vajda, Siberian Landscapes in Ket Traditional Culture

ket_hosedem.name: Bringer of disease, cold and death from the north
ket_hosedem.notes: Banished to the frozen north, the chief evil being sends sickness and misfortune and devours the souls of the dead, the antithesis of warm-south Tomam.

sources.reference: V. I. Anuchin, Ket religion; E. J. Vajda, Siberian Landscapes in Ket Traditional Culture

ket_alba.name: Drove Hosedem northward and burned her in the Arctic
ket_alba.notes: The chief Ket hero pursued the death-goddess down the Yenisei past its mouth into the frozen Arctic sea, where he destroyed her by fire.

sources.reference: E. J. Vajda, Siberian Landscapes in Ket Traditional Culture

ket_alba.name: Cut the channel of the Yenisei
ket_alba.notes: In his pursuit Alba broke through a narrows in the hills and so fixed the course of the Yenisei river through the Ket homeland.

sources.reference: E. J. Vajda, Siberian Landscapes in Ket Traditional Culture

kartvelian_dali.name: Take the form of the wild herd
kartvelian_dali.notes: The huntress can appear as a white or golden ibex or other game animal, marked off from the herd by some sign, to lead or to lure hunters.

sources.reference: K. Tuite, 'The Meaning of Dael: Symbolic and Spatial Associations of the South Caucasian Goddess of Game Animals'

kartvelian_amirani.name: Brought fire and metallurgy to mankind
kartvelian_amirani.notes: Promethean culture-hero who defied the supreme god and gave humankind fire and the working of metals; for his hubris he was chained beneath the Caucasus.

sources.reference: D. Kiziria, 'Amirani, a Georgian Folk Hero'; Georgian Amirani epic (Svan recension)

sources.reference: Javanese wayang kulit puppet iconography of Petruk

sources.reference: Heike Monogatari

kartvelian_ghmerti.gloss: God the Director / the Ruling God

sources.reference: K. Tuite, studies of NE Georgian highland religion; Georgian creation traditions

kalash_balumain.gloss: the Chaumos visitor-hero, a form of Indra

sources.reference: A. Witzel, 'The Religions of the Hindukush'

japanese_yoshiie.name: Veneration as patron of the samurai
japanese_yoshiie.notes: Posthumously honoured as Hachimantarō and revered as a quasi-divine protector of warriors and ancestor-kami of the Minamoto, his cult bound to the Hachiman shrines (notably Iwashimizu Hachimangū).

sources.reference: Ryōjin Hishō; Iwashimizu Hachimangū tradition

javanese_nyai_roro_kidul.name: Labuhan offering to the Queen of the Southern Sea
javanese_nyai_roro_kidul.notes: The Yogyakarta (and Surakarta) court annually casts offerings of royal hair, nail-clippings, garments and food into the southern ocean at Parangkusumo/Parangtritis to renew the mystic pact between the sultans of Mataram and the sea-queen.

sources.reference: Documented Yogyakarta kraton Labuhan ceremony; Mataram-Senopati legend

javanese_sunan_lawu.name: Pilgrimage and vigil on Mount Lawu
javanese_sunan_lawu.notes: Pilgrims ascend to Hargo Dalem and the shrines along the Candi Cetho route to meditate and seek the guardian-spirit's favour, most intensively on the night of 1 Sura (Javanese New Year).

sources.reference: Mount Lawu pilgrimage tradition; Brawijaya V moksha legend

kalash_balumain.name: Chaumos midwinter festival
kalash_balumain.notes: Two-week solstice festival (c. 7-22 Dec.) marking the year's end; Balumain is held to arrive on horseback from Tsiyam to teach and bless the rites, which involve goat sacrifice, juniper purification, dance and song.

sources.reference: A. Witzel, 'The Religions of the Hindukush'; Chaumos festival ethnography

kalash_mahandeo.name: Goat sacrifice at the horse-head altar
kalash_mahandeo.notes: At the wooden four-horse-head altar a goat's throat is cut, the blood splashed on the altar and the head passed back and forth through juniper flame; Mahandeo is the crop-and-war god and intercessor with the highest deity.

sources.reference: Kalash religion ethnography (Chitral valleys); 'before the altar of Mahandeo' field accounts

kalash_sajigor.name: Sacrifice at the open stone altar under junipers
kalash_sajigor.notes: An onjesta ('pure') Indra-aspect god of herds whose stone altar in Rumbur stands beneath old juniper, oak and cedar; goat sacrifice and the pure (onjesta) sphere exclude the impure, women included.

sources.reference: A. Witzel, 'The Religions of the Hindukush'; Kalash religion ethnography

kalash_jestak.name: Clan rites at the Jeshtak-han
kalash_jestak.notes: Weddings, births and ancestral food-offerings are held in the clan's wooden lineage temple (Jeṣṭak Han), one of the few Kalash sanctuaries not barred to women.

sources.reference: A. Witzel, 'The Religions of the Hindukush'; Kalash temple ethnography

karbi_hemphu.name: Rongker village festival
karbi_hemphu.notes: Annual village propitiation led by the Kurusar priest to secure welfare and harvest and avert evil; a fowl is offered to each of Hemphu, Mukrang and Rasinja, who share a common altar.

sources.reference: Karbi Rongker festival ethnography (Karbi Anglong, Assam)

karbi_mukrang.name: Shared sacrifice at the Hemphu-Mukrang-Rasinja altar
karbi_mukrang.notes: Worshipped jointly with Hemphu and his consort Rasinja at a common altar in the Rongker festival, receiving a sacrificial fowl as the war-and-justice member of the Karbi triad.

sources.reference: Karbi Rongker festival ethnography

jukun_aku_uka.name: Puje royal festival
jukun_aku_uka.notes: The divine king presides over the Puje festival of Jukun spirituality, dance and rite; his enthronement requires ritual seclusion and divinization (the Pânkán and Pánkyá rites) before he enters the palace.

sources.reference: C. K. Meek, A Sudanese Kingdom (Jukun of Wukari); Jukun divine-kingship studies

ket_tomam.name: Honoured as bringer of the spring birds
ket_tomam.notes: The warm-south mother is invoked at the return of the migratory waterfowl, whose arrival from her southern land rescues the Ket from late-winter hunger.

sources.reference: E. J. Vajda, Siberian Landscapes in Ket Traditional Culture

attributes.name: Flute-playing youth on Gojō Bridge
attributes.notes: Pictured in art as the slender boy Ushiwakamaru playing his flute by night when he meets and subdues the warrior-monk Benkei on Gojō Bridge.

sources.reference: Ukiyo-e tradition (Yoshitoshi, Kuniyoshi); Gikeiki

attributes.name: Stout androgynous body with topknot and pendulous form
attributes.notes: Depicted short and fat with a flat pug nose, jutting lower jaw, a single tuft/topknot of white hair, a swollen belly and rear and a checkered hip-cloth, the mandatory humble guise of the god Ismaya.

sources.reference: Javanese wayang kulit puppet iconography of Semar

attributes.name: Tall, lanky figure with a very long nose
attributes.notes: The long pointed nose and gangling height are Petruk's defining puppet features, marking the sharp-tongued, witty son of Semar.

sources.reference: Javanese wayang kulit puppet iconography of Petruk

attributes.name: Short club-footed figure with a crippled arm
attributes.notes: Depicted small and misshapen with a club foot and a withered arm and a halting speech, the eldest clown-son of Semar.

sources.reference: Javanese wayang kulit puppet iconography of Gareng

attributes.name: Squat, rotund figure born of Semar's shadow
attributes.notes: The youngest panakawan, depicted short, obese and blunt-featured; in the common Javanese account he was formed from Semar's own shadow to be his companion.

sources.reference: Javanese wayang kulit puppet iconography of Bagong

attributes.name: Sea-green raiment (gadhung mlathi)
attributes.notes: Associated above all with the sacred sea-green colour gadhung mlathi; bathers on the south coast are warned never to wear green lest the queen claim them.

sources.reference: Javanese southern-sea tradition; Nyai Roro Kidul legend

attributes.name: Long golden hair and glowing skin
attributes.notes: A radiant nude woman of surpassing beauty with long golden hair (the seat of her power) and luminous skin, dwelling on inaccessible cliffs.

sources.reference: K. Tuite, 'The Meaning of Dael'
K. Tuite, 'The Meaning of Dael: Symbolic and Spatial Associations of the South Caucasian Goddess of Game Animals'

attributes.name: Sun-and-Moon shoulder marks and golden tooth
attributes.notes: Bore upon his shoulders the images of the Sun and Moon and had a tooth (or teeth) of gold, the bodily signs of his semi-divine birth from the goddess Dali.

sources.reference: Georgian Amirani epic (Svan recension); D. Kiziria, 'Amirani, a Georgian Folk Hero'
Georgian Amirani cycle; Q'ursha ('Black-ear') the dog who licks his chains

attributes.name: The rainbow as Indra's bow
attributes.notes: The rainbow is named 'Indra's bow' as in the Veda, and thunder is Indra at play; Warīn's shrine site was fixed by a bow-shot, echoing the Vedic Indra's bow.

sources.reference: A. Witzel, 'The Religions of the Hindukush'
E. J. Vajda, Siberian Landscapes in Ket Traditional Culture
